mainTopic: Paying a worker in an עיסקא or animal-raising partnership so it is not ריבית, and how and when partners may divide shared property
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining רב עיליש's partnership document: the terms must have been uneven, and that gap paid him for his work, so there was no ריבית. רב זביד suggests a tiny benefit might have been enough, like dipping bread in brine together, following רבי יהודה. רב כהנא answers that רב נחמן never ruled like רבי יהודה. He only showed that three תנאים share one שיטה. Next, רב allows a calf-fattener to be paid with the profit beyond one-third. שמואל requires a fixed דינר instead. The גמרא defends רב against his own 'head of the calf' rule in two ways. The story of רבי אלעזר מהגרוניא and his אריס shows that extra pay is needed only when the owner puts up all the money. Two ברייתות then set how long a raiser must care for an animal and its offspring, and how the offspring are split. אביי rejects רב מנשיא בר גדא's self-made split. Finally, רב פפא rules on two partners who divided money and then wine without consent, and his explanation of the difference continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The second possible reading of רב עיליש's document
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes explaining that the document must have had uneven terms. If the investor took half of any loss, רב עיליש got two-thirds of the profit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if the other side took half of the loss, then רב עיליש got two-thirds of the profit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an explanation that began just before this point. רב עיליש's document must have been set up with uneven terms, and the uneven split paid him for his work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In an עיסקא, part of the money works like a loan. If the worker gets no pay for his effort, the lender's benefit counts as ריבית. Uneven terms, such as half the loss but two-thirds of the profit, give the worker an extra share, and that extra share is his wages.

keyTerms.meaning: profit or earnings (here: באגר, in the profit)

phrases.english: Or, if it was half in the loss,
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from the previous page. The first option was two-thirds of the loss and half of the profit.

phrases.english: then it was two-thirds in the profit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the explanation of רב עיליש's document from the previous page.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the case: the document must have had lopsided terms that paid the worker.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The document seemed to describe a deal where the worker got nothing for his effort, which would be ריבית.
steps.terutzMaskana: The uneven split itself was the worker's pay, so the deal was permitted.

steps.title: רב זביד: maybe a tiny benefit was enough
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד rejects the proof. Maybe רב עיליש's pay was something tiny, like dipping bread in brine with the investor. That would be enough according to רבי יהודה, and רב נחמן ruled like רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: I told this teaching to רב זביד of נהרדעא, and he said to me: Maybe רב עיליש dipped bread in brine together with him? And רב נחמן said the הלכה follows רבי יהודה!
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא reports that he repeated the reasoning about רב עיליש to רב זביד. רב זביד questioned it: the document does not have to have had uneven terms.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי יהודה in the ברייתא on the previous page, even a tiny benefit, like sharing a dip of bread in brine, is enough to count as wages. If רב עיליש received something like that, the document could have had an even split. Since רב נחמן ruled like רבי יהודה, this way of reading the document would be acceptable.

keyTerms.meaning: dips with him in brine (a tiny shared benefit)

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said: I said this teaching

phrases.aramaic: קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב זְבִיד מִנְּהַרְדְּעָא, וַאֲמַר לִי:
phrases.english: before Rav Zevid of Neharde'a, and he said to me:

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא רַב עִילִישׁ טוֹבֵל עִמּוֹ בְּצִיר הֲוָה.
phrases.english: Perhaps Rav Ilish used to dip bread in brine with him.
phrases.notes: This points back to רבי יהודה in the ברייתא on the previous page, who says even this small benefit counts as pay.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה!
phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said: The halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda!

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּלְמָא רַב עִילִישׁ טוֹבֵל עִמּוֹ בְּצִיר הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the explanation in step 1, which assumed the document had to have uneven terms.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the document must have had uneven terms.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: There is another way to pay the worker, a tiny benefit, which is enough according to רבי יהודה. Since רב נחמן ruled like him, uneven terms were not required.

steps.title: רב כהנא: רב נחמן stated a shared approach, not a ruling
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא answers that רב נחמן did not rule like רבי יהודה. He only said that רבי יהודה and the others hold one shared approach (שיטה).
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: A הלכה ruling was not stated. Rather, a 'shared approach' was stated.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא defends the original reasoning. He removes the base of רב זביד's challenge by saying that רב נחמן never actually ruled like רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן's statement was about three תנאים who all hold the same view. He was noting that their opinions are one approach, not deciding that the הלכה follows them. Without a ruling like רבי יהודה, a tiny benefit is not enough, so the uneven-terms explanation stands.

keyTerms.meaning: a shared line of thought held by several sages

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'שיטה' as 'and this is the הלכה'. רב כהנא's point is that רב נחמן was describing these opinions, not ruling like them.

phrases.english: He said to him: It was not stated as a halacha,
rather it was stated as a shared approach.
phrases.notes: He means רבי יהודה, רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל all share the same basic view.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָאו הִלְכְתָא אִיתְּמַר, אֶלָּא שִׁיטָה אִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב זביד's challenge by correcting what רב נחמן actually said.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting what was reported: the statement was a 'שיטה', not a 'הלכה'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב נחמן ruled like רבי יהודה, so a tiny benefit is enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב נחמן only grouped the opinions together. There is no ruling like רבי יהודה, so רבא's explanation holds.

steps.title: Proof from the way רב נחמן listed each name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports רב כהנא. If רב נחמן had meant to rule, he would not have needed to list each sage separately. Saying 'like רבי יהודה', the most lenient one, would have covered everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: This also makes sense. If you don't say so, why did he need to list them and say 'הלכה... הלכה...'? He should have just said: the הלכה follows רבי יהודה, who is the most lenient of them all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a logical proof that רב כהנא is right about what רב נחמן meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבי יהודה is the most lenient, a ruling like him would already cover the cases the stricter sages allow. Listing each name one by one makes no sense as a ruling. It does make sense as a way of showing that the three opinions are one approach.
steps.whatToRemember: רב נחמן did not rule like רבי יהודה. He only showed that three תנאים share one view. So a tiny benefit, like dipping in brine, is not proven to be enough, and רבא's reading of רב עיליש's document stands.

phrases.english: This too stands to reason,
for if you do not say so,
why did he need to list them one by one
and say 'the halacha... the halacha...'?
Let him say: The halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda,
who is the most lenient of them all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב כהנא's answer in step 3 with logic.
steps.raayaObject: That רב נחמן's statement was a 'שיטה', not a ruling.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The wording of רב נחמן's own statement: he named each sage separately instead of naming only the most lenient.

steps.title: רב: the fattener's wages can be the profit beyond one-third
steps.stepSummary: רב says a calf-fattening deal is permitted when the fattener's wages are whatever profit is left over beyond one-third.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: If one says 'the surplus beyond one-third is your wages', this is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: A new discussion begins. רב permits a deal where an owner gives a calf to be fattened, and the fattener's pay comes from the extra profit beyond a set amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Part of the deal works like a loan, so the fattener must be paid for his effort to avoid ריבית. רב holds that promising him the leftover profit beyond one-third counts as real wages.

phrases.english: Rav said: 'The surplus beyond one-third is your wages' —
this is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic on how wages can be set in a partnership.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wages set as the profit beyond one-third are valid wages, so the deal is permitted.

steps.title: שמואל: he may go home with nothing
steps.stepSummary: שמואל objects to רב. If the profit never goes beyond one-third, the fattener gets nothing for his work.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: If he doesn't find a surplus beyond one-third, he goes home empty-handed!
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל attacks רב's ruling by pointing to a case where the fattener ends up with no wages at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wages that depend on profit might never come. In that case the fattener worked for free, and the owner's benefit becomes ריבית. So a pay that is not guaranteed is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: did not find, did not end up with

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: לֹא מָצָא מוֹתַר שְׁלִישׁ,
phrases.english: And Shmuel said: If he did not find a surplus beyond one-third,
shall he go home empty-handed?!

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא מָצָא מוֹתַר שְׁלִישׁ, יֵלֵךְ לְבֵיתוֹ רֵיקָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב's ruling in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that profit beyond one-third counts as wages.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If no such profit comes, the fattener earns nothing, so his work was free and the deal involves ריבית.

steps.title: שמואל: the owner must set a fixed דינר
steps.stepSummary: שמואל gives his own rule. The owner must set a fixed payment of a דינר for the fattener.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, שמואל said: He sets a fixed payment of a דינר for him.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting רב's approach, שמואל says what is needed instead: a fixed, guaranteed wage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A set payment, like a דינר, makes sure the fattener is paid no matter what happens to the profit. This removes the risk that he worked for free, so there is no ריבית.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: profit beyond one-third can serve as wages. שמואל: no, because it might come to nothing. The fattener needs a fixed payment, like a דינר.

phrases.english: Rather, Shmuel said:
He sets a fixed dinar for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: קוֹצֵץ לוֹ דִּינָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives שמואל's alternative after his objection in step 6.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to שמואל, the fattener must get a guaranteed fixed wage (a דינר), not profit that might never come.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to שמואל, the owner must set a fixed payment (a דינר) for the fattener, so he is paid even if there is no profit beyond one-third.

steps.title: Does רב really not require a fixed payment?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב: another statement of his seems to require a guaranteed extra payment, the calf's head.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רב really hold that you don't need to set aside a דינר for the fattener? But רב said the head of the calf goes to the fattener. Isn't that a case where the owner told him: the profit beyond one-third is your wages? So רב also requires something guaranteed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction between two statements of רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 5, רב allowed paying the fattener only with profit beyond one-third, so nothing was guaranteed. But in a different statement רב gives the fattener the calf's head. That sounds like an extra, guaranteed payment, just like שמואל's דינר.

keyTerms.meaning: set aside / fix a set amount
the one who fattens the animal
the profit left over beyond one-third

phrases.aramaic: וְסָבַר רַב אֵין קוֹצְצִין לוֹ דִּינָר?
phrases.english: And does Rav hold that one does not need to set aside a dinar for him?
phrases.notes: This refers back to שמואל's rule in Step 7, that the owner must set a fixed דינר for the fattener.

phrases.english: But didn't Rav say:
The head of the calf goes to the fattener.
Is it not talking about where the owner said to him:
The surplus beyond one-third is your wages?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְסָבַר רַב אֵין קוֹצְצִין לוֹ דִּינָר? וְהָאָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests רב's ruling from Step 5 against שמואל's demand in Step 7, using another statement of רב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that 'surplus beyond one-third' alone is enough pay
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב's own 'head of the calf' rule seems to add a guaranteed payment on top of the surplus. That suggests רב also requires something fixed.

steps.title: The head was an alternative, not an addition
steps.stepSummary: The head of the calf was offered as an either-or option, not as an extra on top of the surplus.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It is where the owner said: either you get the surplus beyond one-third, or you get the head of the calf.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב's 'head of the calf' case is a separate choice of payment. It is not a guaranteed extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the head is just another way to pay, then it is not a guaranteed bonus added to the surplus. So רב's two statements do not clash. He can still hold that surplus beyond one-third alone is fine.

phrases.english: No, it is where he said to him:
Either the surplus beyond one-third,
or the head of the calf to the fattener.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא, דְּקָאָמַר לֵיהּ: אִי מוֹתַר שְׁלִישׁ, אִי רֵישׁ עִגְלָא לְפָטוֹמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the head is an alternative form of pay, not an added guarantee.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The head was a guaranteed payment added to the surplus.
steps.terutzMaskana: The head was one of two choices, so רב never required a fixed extra.

steps.title: Surplus alone is fine when the fattener has his own animal
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: רב allowed 'surplus beyond one-third' only where the fattener already feeds his own animal, so the extra work is small.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: when רב allowed 'the surplus beyond one-third is your wages', it was where the fattener already has an animal of his own. As people say: if you mix feed for one ox, you mix feed for oxen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer. It limits רב's lenient ruling to a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a fattener needs guaranteed pay, as the 'head of the calf' rule shows. But if he is already feeding his own animal, adding one more is barely extra work. So the uncertain surplus is enough pay in that case.

keyTerms.meaning: if you want, say (introduces a second answer)

phrases.english: If you want, say:
When Rav says
that 'the surplus beyond one-third is your wages' is permitted,
it is in a case where he has an animal of his own.
As people say:
Mix feed for an ox, mix feed for oxen.
phrases.notes: Once you're already preparing food for one ox, feeding a second one is hardly any extra effort.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: כִּי קָאָמַר רַב מוֹתַר שְׁלִישׁ בִּשְׂכָרְךָ מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, different answer to the קשיא of Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits רב's lenient ruling to a special case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב allowed surplus-only pay in every case.
steps.terutzMaskana: Surplus-only pay is allowed only when the fattener already feeds his own animal, so his extra work is minimal.
steps.whatToRemember: Two answers for רב: (1) the head was an either-or option, or (2) surplus-only pay works when the fattener already has his own animal to feed.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר מהגרוניא and his sharecropper
steps.stepSummary: A story: רבי אלעזר paid his אריס the head plus half the profit. Later, when the אריס became a partner, he offered half the tail but asked to split the head.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר מהגרוניא bought an animal and gave it to his אריס to fatten. He gave him the head as wages plus half the profit. The אריס's wife told him: if you became his partner, he would also give you the tail. So he went and bought an animal together with רבי אלעזר. רבי אלעזר gave him part of the tail, and then said: come, let's split the head.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows these rules in real life. It sets up the אריס's complaint in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first the אריס did not invest any money, so he got the full head as wages plus half the profit. Once he invested as a partner, רבי אלעזר treated him as an equal: shared tail, shared head. This change is what the אריס will question next.

keyTerms.meaning: sharecropper / worker who tends an owner's property for a share
the fat tail of the animal

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar of Hagronya bought an animal,
and gave it to his sharecropper to fatten it,
and gave him the head as his wages,
and gave him half the profit.
His wife said to him:
phrases.notes: This is the sharecropper's wife talking to her husband.

phrases.english: If you would become a partner with him,
he would give you the tail too.
He went and bought an animal together with him.
He gave him a share of the tail.
He said to him: Come, let us split the head.
phrases.notes: Here רבי אלעזר is the one speaking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the rulings of רב and שמואל to a practical story about paying a fattener.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A non-investing fattener got the head plus half the profit. Once he became a partner, everything was split evenly.

steps.title: The sharecropper complains
steps.stepSummary: The אריס asks why, now that he is a partner, he should get less of the head than before.
steps.simpleTranslation: The אריס said: Now I don't even get what I got at the beginning?
steps.whatsHappening: The אריס challenges רבי אלעזר. Becoming a partner seems to have made his deal worse, not better.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, he got the whole head. Now he gets only half of it. He expected that investing his own money would add benefits, not take away the head he used to get.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Now, not even what I got at the beginning?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to רבי אלעזר's offer to split the head.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's decision to split the head once they became partners
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Investing money should not leave the אריס worse off than when he invested nothing and got the whole head.

steps.title: Extra pay was only to avoid the look of interest
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains that the extra pay was needed before so it would not look like רבית. Now, as partners, the small extra work is normal for a sharecropper.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר answered: Until now the money was all mine. If I had not given you a little extra, it would look like רבית. Now we are partners. What can you say, that you work a little harder? People say: an ordinary אריס commits himself to bring the landowner pasture.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the אריס's complaint and explains why the deal changed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When רבי אלעזר owned all the money, the fattener's work without enough pay would be like a benefit for the loan, which looks like רבית. So he had to give extra. Now they both invested, so there is no loan and no רבית problem. The little extra work the אריס does is simply what sharecroppers normally do for the owner.
steps.whatToRemember: Extra pay for a fattener is needed only when the owner put up all the money, so it won't look like רבית. Between true partners, splitting evenly is fine.
steps.whyThisMatters: This story shows the reason behind the earlier rules of רב and שמואל. The guaranteed payment exists to keep the deal from looking like a loan with interest.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Until now the money was mine.

phrases.aramaic: אִי לָא הֲוָה יָהֵיבְנָא לָךְ טְפֵי פּוּרְתָּא –
phrases.english: If I had not given you a little more,
it would look like interest.
Now we are partners.
What would you say?
'I work a little harder'?
People say:
An ordinary sharecropper, for the owner of the land,
commits himself to bring him pasture.
phrases.notes: Sharecroppers normally do a bit of extra work for the owner, so a little more effort doesn't earn extra pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the אריס's complaint in Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the reason for the original extra pay, and shows that reason no longer applies.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole head was a fixed benefit that the אריס keeps no matter what.
steps.terutzMaskana: The head was only to avoid the look of רבית when the owner put up all the money. As partners, an even split is correct.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A guaranteed extra for the fattener is needed only when the owner funds the whole animal. Equal partners split evenly.

steps.title: How long the raiser must care for the animal
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: סומכוס says the raiser must care for female donkeys 18 months and flocks 24 months. Neither side can divide early.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: If someone gives an animal to his friend to raise, how long must the friend care for it? סומכוס says: female donkeys, eighteen months; flocks of sheep or goats, twenty-four months. If one of them wants to divide before the time is up, the other can stop him, but the care in one year is not like the care in another year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that sets the default length of the deal when the two partners did not say how long it would last.
steps.deeperAnalysis: סומכוס gives fixed times for each kind of animal. During that time, either partner can block the other from selling and splitting early. The last line, starting with 'אבל', sounds strange, and the גמרא will deal with it next.

keyTerms.meaning: One who values an animal and gives it to a friend to raise for shared profit

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
One who appraises an animal for his fellow,
phrases.notes: He sets a price on the animal and gives it to his friend to raise, and they share the profit.

phrases.english: until when is he obligated to care for it?
Sumchos says:
For female donkeys, eighteen months;
for flocks, twenty-four months.
And if one comes to divide within its time,
phrases.notes: He wants to sell the animal and split the profit before the time is up.

phrases.english: his fellow can stop him,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אֵינוֹ דּוֹמֶה טִיפּוּלָהּ שֶׁל שָׁנָה זוֹ
phrases.english: but the care of this year is not like
the care of another year.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the story of רבי אלעזר to a new ברייתא about the length of an animal-raising deal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Default care period: 18 months for donkeys, 24 months for flocks. Neither side may divide early.

steps.title: The word 'but' does not fit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word 'אבל' means in the ברייתא, since it does not make sense there.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is this word 'but' saying?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the word 'but' does not fit the flow of the ברייתא. This sets up a fix to the wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'But' should introduce a contrast to the rule before it. Here, the last line actually gives the reason for the rule, so 'but' sounds wrong.

phrases.english: "But" — what is it saying?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the ברייתא of סומכוס.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word 'אבל' at the end of סומכוס's ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The line does not contrast with the rule. It explains it, so 'but' does not fit.

steps.title: Read it as 'because'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the wording: the partner can stop an early split because each year's care is different.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, read it as: because the care of this year is not like the care of another year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording so the last line becomes the reason why the partner can block an early split.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Caring for the animal is harder in some years and easier in others. If they split partway, one side may have done the hard part without getting the benefit. So each side can insist on finishing the full period.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, here used to correct the wording
Its care, the work of tending it

phrases.english: Rather:

phrases.aramaic: לְפִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ דּוֹמֶה טִיפּוּלָהּ שֶׁל שָׁנָה זוֹ
phrases.english: because the care of this year is not like
the care of another year.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about 'אבל' by changing it to 'לפי ש'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the wording of the text
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'But' looked like it limited the rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: The line is the reason for the rule: each year's care is different, so neither side can end early.

steps.title: How long the raiser must care for the offspring
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא: the raiser cares for offspring of small animals 30 days and large animals 50 days. רבי יוסי says small animals need three months.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: If someone gives an animal to his friend to raise, how long must the friend care for the babies? Small animals, thirty days; large animals, fifty days. רבי יוסי says: small animals, three months, because they need a lot of care.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא, this time about how long the raiser must care for the babies born to the animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion gives small animals a shorter time than large ones. רבי יוסי disagrees and gives small animals three months, because they need more care.

phrases.english: It is taught in another one:
One who appraises an animal for his fellow,
until when is he obligated to care for the offspring?
For small animals, thirty days;
and for large animals, fifty days.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: בַּדַּקָּה שְׁלֹשָׁה חֳדָשִׁים,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says: For small animals, three months,
because its care is great.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the mother animal to the care of its offspring.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Offspring care: 30 days for small animals, 50 for large. רבי יוסי says three months for small animals.

steps.title: Why do small animals need more care?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי יוסי means by 'a lot of care'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'its care is great' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask what extra care רבי יוסי is talking about. This sets up the answer in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It seems odd that small animals would need more care than large ones. So the גמרא asks what makes them harder to raise.

phrases.english: What is 'its care is great'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for an explanation of רבי יוסי's reason.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra care small animals need

steps.title: Their teeth are thin
steps.stepSummary: Small animals have thin teeth, so they need extra help eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because its teeth are thin.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the babies of small animals have thin, weak teeth, so feeding them takes more work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because their teeth are thin, the raiser must prepare their food, for example by cutting it up. That extra work is why רבי יוסי gives a longer time.

phrases.english: because its teeth are thin.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about 'a lot of care'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Small animals have thin teeth, so feeding them takes extra work.

steps.title: How the offspring are divided afterward
steps.stepSummary: After the care period, the raiser takes his own half plus half of his partner's half.
steps.simpleTranslation: From then on, he takes his own half, and half of his friend's half.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues: once the care period is over, the offspring are divided.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The raiser owns half, so he takes half of the offspring. He also takes half of the owner's half, which is a quarter of the total, as pay for his work. In the end he has three quarters.

keyTerms.meaning: Half of a half, one quarter

steps.confusionAlert: 'Half of his friend's half' is not an extra half. It is a quarter of the whole, so the raiser ends with three quarters and the owner with one quarter.

phrases.english: From here on,
he takes his own half,
and half of the half of his fellow's share.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא after the short explanation of 'a lot of care'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After the care period, the raiser takes half the offspring plus a quarter as pay.

steps.title: רב מנשיא בר גדא divides the offspring
steps.stepSummary: רב מנשיא בר גדא took his half plus a quarter of the offspring, and the case came before אביי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מנשיא בר גדא took his half and half of his friend's half. The case came before אביי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story of someone who divided the offspring just as the ברייתא describes. This sets up אביי's reaction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He seems to follow the ברייתא exactly. The question is whether he was allowed to do it himself, and the next lines show the problem.

phrases.english: Rav Menashya bar Gadda
took his half
and half of the half of his fellow's share.
It came before Abaye.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב מְנַשְּׁיָא בַּר גַּדָּא שְׁקַל מֶחֱצָה שֶׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A real case applying the division rule from the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב מנשיא בר גדא divided the offspring himself: his half plus a quarter.

steps.title: Who divided it for you?
steps.stepSummary: אביי objects that רב מנשיא divided on his own, without anyone overseeing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Who divided it for you?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רב מנשיא for doing the split by himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the math is right, one partner should not divide shared property on his own. He might not choose fairly which animals go to whom.

phrases.english: He said to him: Who divided it for you?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: אביי's first objection to רב מנשיא's action.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב מנשיא's dividing the offspring on his own
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A partner may not divide shared property by himself. It needs a fair, agreed split.

steps.title: The local custom is to keep raising
steps.stepSummary: אביי adds that this is a place where the custom is to keep raising the offspring, and a משנה says to follow that custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, this is a place where the custom is to raise the offspring, and we learned in a משנה: In a place where the custom is to raise, they should raise.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a second objection: in this place, people do not split the offspring at all, they keep raising them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The division rule in the ברייתא only applies where there is no custom to keep raising. Here there was such a custom, and a משנה says to follow it. So רב מנשיא should not have divided at all.

keyTerms.meaning: A place where the custom is

steps.whatToRemember: Local custom decides how an animal-raising deal works. The ברייתא's split applies only where there is no custom to keep raising, and a partner may never divide on his own.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that in business deals, local custom can override the default rules a ברייתא sets.

phrases.english: And furthermore:
it is a place where they are accustomed to raise,
phrases.notes: The custom there is that the raiser keeps raising the babies too, instead of splitting them.

phrases.english: and we learned:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה on the next page, דף ס״ט ע״ב.

phrases.english: A place where they are accustomed to raise, they should raise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, stronger objection from אביי, backed by a משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב מנשיא's choice to divide the offspring at all
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Where the custom is to keep raising the offspring, a משנה says to follow it, so there should be no split.

steps.title: Two partners, and one splits the money without asking
steps.stepSummary: Two כותאי ran a joint business. One of them split the money without the other's knowledge, and they came to רב פפא.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were two Samaritans who did business together. One of them went and divided the money without his partner knowing. They came to רב פפא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story about two partners. This line sets up the case, and רב פפא's ruling comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, אביי objected to רב מנשיא for dividing on his own, with no one overseeing it. This story tests a related question: what happens when one partner divides shared money without the other partner's consent?

phrases.english: There were these two Samaritans
who made a business venture with each other.
One of them went and divided the money
without the knowledge of his partner.
They came before רב פפא.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ תְּרֵי כּוּתָאֵי דַּעֲבוּד עִסְקָא בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After אביי's objection to dividing without oversight, the גמרא brings a related story about a partner dividing without consent.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Case setup: one partner divided the shared money without the other's knowledge.

steps.title: רב פפא: dividing money changes nothing
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא tells the complaining partner he lost nothing, because רב נחמן taught that money is already considered divided.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to him: What difference does it make? This is what רב נחמן said: Money is considered as if it were already divided.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא rules that the partner who divided the money did nothing wrong. He bases this on a teaching of רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every coin is the same, so splitting money in half cannot cheat anyone. Each partner's half was already clearly his own share, so dividing it without permission causes no loss.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule about money sets up the contrast with the wine case that comes next.

phrases.english: He said to him: What difference does it make?
phrases.notes: רב פפא is talking to the partner who complained. He means: what did you lose?

phrases.english: This is what רב נחמן said:
Money is like something already divided.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי נָפְקָא מִינַּהּ? הָכִי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רב פפא's ruling on the case set up in step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dividing shared money without the partner's consent is valid, since money is considered already divided (רב נחמן).

steps.title: The next year: the other partner splits the wine, and רב פפא objects
steps.stepSummary: The same partners bought wine together. The other partner divided it without consent, and this time רב פפא challenged him: who divided it for you?
steps.simpleTranslation: The next year they bought wine together. The other partner got up and divided it without his partner knowing. They came before רב פפא. He said to him: Who divided it for you?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story about the same partners. This time the shared item is wine, and רב פפא does not approve of the division.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the surface, this case looks just like the money case: one partner divided without the other's consent. But רב פפא now rules the opposite way. The reason for the difference has not been given yet, which is exactly why the next complaint comes.
steps.confusionAlert: This time it is the OTHER partner who divides. That is why he later feels that רב פפא always rules against him.

phrases.english: The next year they bought wine together.
The other one got up and divided it
without the knowledge of his partner,
they came before רב פפא.
He said to him: Who divided it for you?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, similar case in which רב פפא rules the opposite way from step 25.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dividing shared wine without the partner's consent is not accepted.

steps.title: The partner complains that רב פפא is picking on him
steps.stepSummary: The partner accuses רב פפא of ruling against him both times, even though the two cases seem the same. רב פפא begins to reply.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I see that the Master is coming after me! רב פפא said:
steps.whatsHappening: The partner who lost both cases challenges רב פפא for being inconsistent. The last words, 'רב פפא said,' set up his answer, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The complaint is really a question of consistency. Last year, dividing without consent was fine, so why is it wrong now? רב פפא must explain what makes wine different from money.

keyTerms.meaning: you are coming after me (picking on me)
the Master (a respectful way to address a rabbi)

phrases.english: He said to him: I see
that the Master is coming after me!
phrases.notes: He feels singled out: last year his partner won by dividing, and now he loses for doing the same thing.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:

steps.triggerLanguage: קָא חָזֵינָא דְּבָתַר דִּידִי קָא אָתֵי מָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the apparent contradiction between רב פפא's rulings in steps 25 and 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's opposite rulings in the money case and the wine case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both cases involve one partner dividing without consent, so the rulings should match. Ruling differently looks like bias against this partner.
